newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ mortgage rates under upward pressure-Countrywide.
newsitem.headline: NZ mortgage rates under upward pressure-Countrywide.

text.p: Countrywide Bank, owned by Bank of Scotland Plc, said on Thursday it would have to consider raising its New Zealand floating mortgage rates if there was not an imminent fall in wholesale market bank bill rates.
"We are not yet convinced that floating rates will have to increase, but current monetary conditions are strongly suggesting they will," managing director David Wolfenden said in a statement.
The bank is keeping what it calls a watching brief on its floating interest rate, which currently stands at 8.95 percent -- at the same level as most major lenders in the market.

Recent increases in the benchmark 90-day bank bill rate, which has risen to around 7.70 percent this week from just over 7.0 percent in June, have surprised many home lenders who say they anticipated relative stability, or a downward trend, in New Zealand rates when they last cut their rates.
Economic fundamentals appear to confirm that there is a benign inflationary outlook and all the preconditions for lower interest rates.

But an increase in the 90-day bill rate to 7.74 percent during Thursday "meant that the bank would have to consider raising its floating rate if a reduction in (that) rate was not imminent," Countrywide said.
Wolfenden noted that his bank had led major banks down in the last three mortgage rate reductions in New Zealand.
"While we prefer to hold a long-term view on interest rates and to invest in future benfits to our customers, current volatility means we have to be ready to act quickly," he added.

The bank was concerned that the current stance of the Reserve Bank of New Zealand, which implements a monetary policy intended to keep core inflation within a zero to three percent band, was tending to produce a strong case for higher interest rates to offset a weakened dollar.
Yet this situation was coinciding with inflation at a 10-year low, and some economic indicators showing the economy "teetering on the edge of recession", Wolfenden said.
"Unfortunately, the government is not providing strong leadership or wisdom for the future direction of the New Zealand economy, particularly fiscal management," he added.
"Home owners may end up paying a price for that in increased rates".
Other bankers contacted by Reuters have said they share this concern over mortgage rates and that an upward move by one lender is likely to spark a rapid knock-on among the others.
